title: No sound of iron (1 Kings 6:7)
hook: the Temple is built without the sound of hammer or axe

segments.voice: Yesterday, two mothers, a sword, and rachamim. Your line was the real mother gives way. Did you let one point go to save something bigger? Today, the Temple goes up, quietly. Day seven hundred fifty-nine.

A building site is loud. Saws, drills, a radio, somebody shouting measurements across the lot. One verse in the book of Kings describes a building site of a different kind: Solomon's house for God in Jerusalem. Great stones are going up, cedar beams, gold. And right in the middle of the description, the text stops to tell us something that sounds like an aside. At the site itself, you couldn't hear the hammers. Not because nobody cut stone. Because the cutting happened somewhere else. Today's word is that silence.
screen: `A BUILDING SITE IS LOUD.` → `SOLOMON'S HOUSE FOR GOD.` → `YOU COULDN'T HEAR THE HAMMERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, First Kings six, verse seven. The house was built of stone made ready before it was brought, and there was "neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house, while it was in building." The Hebrew word for iron is barzel. The cutting happened at the quarry. At the holy place, the stones were only set. Why tell us? The verse doesn't say. But some readers hear an echo from the Torah. In Exodus, an altar of stone is to be built of stones no tool has been lifted against; lift your tool on it, the text says, and you have profaned it. A later Jewish teaching in the Mishnah gives a reason: iron was made to shorten a person's life, and the altar was made to lengthen it, so the thing that shortens shouldn't be raised over the thing that lengthens. And the Talmud tells a legend of the shamir, a tiny creature that could cut stone without any tool, so the work could go on in silence. That one is a story the rabbis tell, not a line in Kings. Set side by side, these readings point the same way: the metal that can shorten a life is kept away from the place built to lengthen it. The noise happened offstage, in the quarry. Here, there was only placing, fitting, setting. There's a kind of work like that in ordinary life. The kind where you don't announce yourself. The preparation done out of sight. The kind that's finished before anyone hears it. In this verse, the Temple is built that way.
screen: `STONE MADE READY AT THE QUARRY.` · `NO TOOL LIFTED ON THE ALTAR.` · `IRON SHORTENS, THE ALTAR LENGTHENS.` · `THE SHAMIR: A LEGEND OF SILENCE.` · then, large: `NEITHER HAMMER NOR AXE NOR ANY TOOL OF IRON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: work quietly today. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one task waiting for you: a sink of dishes, a report, a phone call, a favor for someone. Now see yourself doing it the Temple way: the preparation done beforehand, the work itself done without announcing it, without telling anyone how hard it was. No sighing, no posting, no complaint. Let this quiet minute be the quarry, where you get ready. If you pray, you can offer the work before you begin it. The bell holds the time.
Barzel. The Hebrew word for iron, the one tool and sound kept away from building the Temple. Today's word.
Your line: finished before anyone hears it. Today, do one good piece of work without announcing it, and let it be finished before anyone hears. Day seven hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Jews read of the Temple's building in the book of Kings, and the Mishnah's teaching about iron and the altar is studied in tractate Middot.

notes: Verify JPS 1917 wording at 1 Kings 6:7 (the quoted clause matches the KJV; JPS may say 'made ready at the quarry').
Mishnah Middot 3:4: iron created to shorten life, the altar to lengthen it; confirm the paraphrase.
The shamir legend: Gittin 68a and Sotah 48b; confirm citations and that it is presented as legend.
Exodus altar verse numbering differs between Hebrew (20:22) and some English Bibles (20:25).
